extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and statesmen researching early American history, law, and institutions
extracted.subtask_short: studying early American laws and sources
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and understand the principal legal rules, voting qualifications, inheritance practices, and recommended primary sources for studying the early United States and its colonies, as summarized in a historical appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sabbath restrictions and enforcement (Massachusetts / early colonial laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions and penalties governing behavior on the Sabbath: restrictions on sporting, fishing, playing games, frequenting places where liquor is sold; limits on travel except in cases of necessity; local officials (tithing-men) may judge travelers' reasons and levy fines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and enforcement mechanisms cited: a Massachusetts law (Law of the 5th March, 1792) provided for fining a traveler five pounds sterling if his reason for travel was not deemed sufficient by the tithing-men, with possible referral to the justice of the peace; later laws (e.g., New York revised statutes) similarly prohibited various activities on the Sabbath and allowed travel only for necessity. The author notes that although such penal provisions often remained on the books, they were likely rarely applied in practice; the strong social regard for the Sabbath nevertheless produced marked effects in city life (e.g., suspension of social movements on Saturday evening).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaming law in New York (penalties and recovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: New York revised statute: 'Whoever shall win or lose in the space of twenty-four hours, by gaming or betting, the sum of twenty-five dollars, shall be found guilty of a misdemeanor, and, upon conviction, shall be condemned to pay a fine equal to at least five times the value of the sum lost or won; which will be paid to the inspector of the poor of the township.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional provisions: a person who loses twenty-five dollars or more may bring an action to recover them; if he neglects to do so, the inspector of the poor may prosecute the winner and oblige him to pay into the poor box both the sum he has gained and three times as much besides. (Quoted from Revised Statutes, part i., chapter 20, p. 675.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of voter qualifications in the United States (circa early 19th century)
rubrics_metrics.description: General rule and state-by-state variations for the right to vote: all states grant the vote at age twenty-one and require a residency period (varying from three months to two years); additional qualifications differ by state and may be property, income, militia service, tax payment, or absence from poor lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-specific qualifications listed in the text: Massachusetts — income of three pounds sterling or capital of sixty pounds; Rhode Island — landed property amounting to $133; Connecticut — property giving an income of $17 (a year of militia service also confers the elective privilege); New Jersey — property of fifty pounds a year; South Carolina and Maryland — possession of fifty acres of land; Tennessee — must possess some property; Mississippi, Ohio, Georgia, Virginia, Pennsylvania, Delaware, New York — paying the taxes is the only necessary qualification (militia service often equivalent to tax payment); Maine and New Hampshire — any man not on the pauper list can vote; Missouri, Alabama, Illinois, Louisiana, Indiana, Kentucky, Vermont — conditions of voting have no reference to the elector's property. Special case: North Carolina applies different conditions for voting for the senate (possess fifty acres) and for the house of representatives (only payment of taxes required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of inheritance and entail in the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: American intestate succession and testamentary freedom: if a man dies intestate, his property goes to his heirs in a direct line; if one heir, that heir succeeds to the whole; if several heirs of same degree, they divide equally without distinction of sex. Testators generally have entire liberty to dispose of property by will, except they may not leave it to a political body or corporation. Entails were largely abolished or modified in many states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origins and statutory milestones: the New York statute of 23 February 1780 first prescribed equal division rules; Vermont is an exception where the male heir inherits a double portion. Entails (estates tail) were abolished in Virginia (1770), New York (1786), and later in North Carolina, Kentucky, Tennessee, Georgia, and Missouri; some states never introduced entails (Vermont, Indiana, Illinois, South Carolina, Louisiana). Some American republics still admit entails under certain restrictions; by contrast, French law prohibits entail in all cases. Commentary: American principles 'tend to favor the free circulation of property.' (References: Kent's Commentaries, vol. i & iv.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended documentary sources and authorities for studying American colonial and state history
rubrics_metrics.description: A short catalogue of the most important works and documents recommended for consultation when researching the history and institutions of the United States and its colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works highlighted and their utility (as described in the text): Ebenezer Hazard, An Historical Collection of State Papers (contains charters and principal colonial acts; vols. 1–2, Philadelphia 1792); Captain John Smith, The Generall Historic of Virginia and New England (1627) — early firsthand narrative of 1584–1626, valued for simple, concise style and credible descriptions; Beverley — narrative 1585–1700 with documents and pictures of Indians and Virginians' manners; William Stith, The History of Virginia (useful but long/diffuse); John Lawson, The History of Carolina (1718) — journey, descriptions of mortality and indigenous customs, physical condition and productions, charter copy; Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society (first printed 1792, reprinted 1806) — contains many valuable and otherwise unpublished documents; Nathaniel Norton's New England's Memorial (reprinted Boston 1826); Cotton Mather, Magnalia Christi Americana (ecclesiastical history 1620–1698) — seven-book division covering foundation, governors, ministers, Cambridge University, church principles, providential accounts, heresies; Hutchinson, History of the Colony of Massachusetts — detailed narrative 1628–1750; Benjamin Trumbull, Complete History of Connecticut (1630–1764); Jeremy Belknap, History of New Hampshire (Boston 1792); William Smith, History of New York (1737) — account of French-English wars and Iroquois confederation; Robert Proud, History of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia 1797) — documents concerning Penn and Quakers. The author gives brief notes on the character, scope, and value of each work to guide selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation on penal law persistence vs. practical enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws, especially penal provisions rooted in early emigrant morals, often remain inflexible on the statute books long after social manners have changed; consequently, penal parts of some laws are very rarely applied despite their continued existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's commentary: although the quoted laws are of recent date (relative to the writing) they are 'unintelligible without going back to the very origin of the colonies.' He adds 'I have no doubt that in our days the penal part of these laws is very rarely applied.' This cautions readers and researchers to distinguish between written statutory provisions and their contemporary enforcement or social effect.
